fatal_errors: The proposed aging-and-precipitation intervention does not reconstruct the target high-energy ball milling plus spark-plasma-sintering route.

It attributes strengthening primarily to newly formed precipitates, whereas the target mechanism is dominated by nanocrystalline grain-boundary strengthening, milling-induced dislocation density and lattice strain, solid-solution strengthening, densification, and an FCC/BCC phase mixture.
The aging temperature and time needed to produce precipitates in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are unspecified, so the intervention is not reproducible.
Treating failure to form precipitates as falsification is invalid: it may only show that the selected aging treatment failed to realize the proposed mediator.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the central strength–ductility tradeoff and supplies a sensible matched comparison using microscopy, diffraction, hardness, strength, and ductility measurements. It is therefore a scientifically plausible alternative rather than unsupported speculation. However, it misses nearly all target-specific processing and structural details: 1–6 h milling at 400 rpm and 20:1 ball-to-powder ratio, SPS at 900–1000 °C for 10 min, nanocrystalline grains below 48 nm, high densification, and the approximately 83% FCC/17% BCC structure. Its predicted outcome is only directional and omits the target values of about 675 HV, 1238 MPa yield stress, and 1894 MPa compressive strength. The cited evidence supports the general proposition that decomposition, fine precipitates, grain refinement, and dislocation density can affect HEA strength, but it concerns AlCoFeNi/AlCoCrFeNi and CoCrFeMnNi rather than aged CoCrFeNiTi, so transfer to the proposed alloy and treatment is indirect. A valid falsification test would first verify comparable precipitate formation, then ask whether precipitate size or volume fraction correlates with strengthening relative to controls that separate grain growth, phase fraction, and density effects.
